pumped up with your strength. Hence making it a characteristic melee
weapon, actually more so. Unlike a junky sword, a chainsaw actually tears
away chunks of the target. Tap me with your sword, you cut me, hit me
*real* hard with your sword, maybe you will chop off part of my body. Tap

rely on strength to go through their target. Kinda like clawing someone
with a meat hook, the hook hurts, the harder you hit with the hook the more

with a non-strength-based melee weapon like Gas-Powered Chainsaw.

ammo cards (unless I misremember something). But one could, in future, print
non-ammo cards that reference "guns" and then the term "gun" would no longer
"mean" merely "usable with ammo cards". It does not necessarily mean that even
now, because we have a weapon, Zip Gun, that cannot use ammo cards. For Zip
Gun, the gun designation has no game relevence as yet, but this would change
if, for instance, a minion were printed that did +1 damage when striking with a
gun.

"Werewolf" means applicable to cards that reference werewolves.

"Mortal" means applicable to cards that reference mortals, etc. etc.

There are no cards as yet which reference Changelings, or Zombies, or Hunters,
or Mages. This will change, and only then will these designations have
practical "meaning", which will continue to be subject to revision with the
printing of each new relevant card.

damage to Kiasid". The term "Cold Iron Vulnerability" on a Kiasid means merely

more cards are printed.

Good reason: Keep errata to a minimum.

Of course, it is conceivable that TC could be reprinted in the Camarilla set
with revised text. Card text updates are not as bad as errata, but, in the
interest of avoiding confusion, it might be better to keep this to a minimum as
well. OTOH, having all Chainsaws in use be of a similar nature also avoids
confusion.

Personally, I feel that the failure of chainsaws to benefit from usual Melee
Weapon enhancers is thematically appropriate as a representation of their
clumsiness. A sword is clearly a superior weapon for someone who knows how to
use it. It seems ok to me that swords can benefit from Lucky Blow, whereas
chainsaws cannot.

Same goes for Undead Strength or Pushing the Limit. I am aware that it takes a
significant amount of (mortal) strength to make full effective use of a
Chainsaw, but I do not think that supernatural strength would add much
additional benefit. I think if you used supernatural strength on a chainsaw,
you would only succeed in breaking it.

Mortal Allies do have different strength levels, ranging from 0 to 4. However
chainsaw damage is unaffected by these figures, whether classified as a melee
weapon or no. Therefore the argument that it takes a certain level of strength
to effectively use a chainsaw (say Strength 1 as opposed to Strength 0), seems
to me hardly relevant to the "melee weapon" issue.

Even Strength 0 ought to be adequate for to make full use of chainsaws. This
is a game where an entire street gang of muscular mortals gets a strength of 1
(or even 0 in the case of The Slashers). So when an internet-posting card
player reports that, in his experience, it does indeed take considerable
strength to make full use of a chainsaw, this hardly proves that one gains
additional benefit from chainsaws by boosting strength up to 2.or 3.

When exceptional mortals have high strength, such as Muddles, this is arguably
more representative of skill (or built-in weaponry) than brute force. Thus, it
is appropriate that they gain little benefit from Chainsaws, in which one is
not likely to receive, nor benefit from, martial training. In Wilbur
Delburton's case (+2 strength with melee weapons) the bonus clearly is related
to skill. Wilbur can make use his bonus with Gas-Powered Chainsaw (striking
for 5!) but it is not clear that he should. Thematically, it seems only right
that clumsy chainsaws should not gain much benefit from skill, speed, training,
or finesse.

-- John Whelan.

I realize you are just being sarcastic, but in defense of the English language
and logic, I feel compelled to point out that, while one may fire a bow during
a skirmish, one is very unlikely to fire it in a melee. This is because the
term "melee" strongly implies mixed combat. Therefore, one does not do this
for fear of hitting ones own troops.

Your dictionary indicates that "skirmish" and "melee" are synonyms - but like
most synonyms this is merely approximate, not precise. You can't play "six
degrees of Kevin Bacon" with synonyms in search of a definition that will
support your argument. Examining the two definitions you provide we see the
following differences:

"Melee" indicates mixed combat, whereas "skirmish" carries no such implication.

"Skirmish" indicates a small-scale engagement, whereas "melee" carries no such
implication.

Bows may be suitable for (non-melee) skirmishes, but not for melees. It is
about as far from being a "melee weapon" as you can get. Same goes for any
ranged weapon (though pistols are arguably more suitable than bows).

I don't mean to take your opponent's side in this debate. Chainsaws are not
really suitable for melee combat nor for any sort of combat - except perhaps
against extremely stupid and slow-moving zombies. As far as I am concerned,
the rules/design teams can classify them any way they choose. Indeed, I agree
with LSJ that it would be thematically best if all chainsaws were simply
"weapons". This is not based on the proper definition of "melee", but rather
because I consider it thematically appropriate that chainsaws not benefit from
the bonuses currently granted to "melee weapons" by other cards. It is
entirely appropriate that it be far less flexible, by having fewer additional
options, than a bastard sword.

range. Real western gunfighters often used their pistols by pushing
the muzzle against the target's body before firing - because there's a
good chance they'd miss at any greater distance.

touching distance - within one meter. Melee is 1-2 meters. Ranged
combat depends upon the effective range of the weapon, e.g. up to 70
yards for a .44 magnum (optimistic, IMO). There are three
corresponding talents and skills:

Brawl - Boxing, Wrestling, Dirty Fighting, Karate, Judo, etc
Melee - Knives, Swords, Improvised Clubs, Stakes, Disarms?, Axes

of all forms, from swords and clubs to esoteric martial-arts
paraphernalia such as sai or nunchaku." It seems no great stretch for
this to cover a chainsaw too though you should perhaps ought to have a
couple of dots in "Crafts" so that you know how to operate one.

VTES doesn't cover these skills, talents and knowledges though. These
might make interesting cards along the lines of the discipline
masters. They might give cost discounts (e.g. your laptop is free if
you have computer skill) or improve the effectiveness of relevant
types of equipment (e.g. +2 intercept for a sports bike if you have

fighting, then it is a *really* bad idea to throw it away.

enemy before closing, plus one (or perhaps two) for fighting hand to hand.

his weapons deprives the distinction of significance.

vampires and the theme is fundamental.

What difference? I hope you mean the spelling.

"Melee" and "Mellay" are the same word. They mean the same. They are
pronounced the same. "Mellay" is an obsolete spelling.

Melee is a French word which is pronounced "mellay." Modern usage favors the
French spelling over an earlier English phoneticization. "Mellay" is still one
of the accepted pronunciations of melee, though, for understandable reasons, it
is often pronounced "m'lee" or "mee-lee"

The OED, for some strange reason, classifies them separately, and provides
different definitions (which pretty much amount to the same thing, except that
the one for "mellay" is more informative). But this differentiation is not
very defensible. Any modern user who wishes to exress the concept defined in
"mellay" will use the modern spelling "melee". Likewise, any bad speller who
writes "melee" phonetically will write "mellay".

Miriam-Websters classification makes more sense. Their definition for "Mellay"
is "= 1st MELEE, 1" which in turn is given as "a fight between combatants
mingled in a confused mass; a skirmish; a fray; an affray"

Why do you keep arguing with this guy and maneuvering yourself into
indefensible positions? He is wrong to try to impose the dictionary on the
game of Jyhad. But he is, for the most part, right about the meaning of the
word "melee" and the phrase "melee weapon". Assuming it means anything at all,
it means a non-ranged weapon for close-quarters hand-to-hand fighting. In the
gaming field, at least, it has been used to mean that for at least 20 years.
Challenging this will achieve nothing except the reduce the term to
meaninglessness and uselessness (except for Jyhad game purposes, of course,
where no definition is required).

-- John Whelan
